definition: Populism is a political style or discourse characterized by an emphasis on the direct connection between 'the people' and their leader or movement, often framing politics as a struggle between the virtuous, authentic 'common people' and a corrupt, out-of-touch elite or establishment. Populist rhetoric typically employs emotional appeals, simplifies complex issues into us-versus-them narratives, criticizes elites or institutions, and claims to represent the true will of the ordinary citizens against the corrupt or disconnected ruling class.
inclusion_criteria: A document is classified as populist if it employs rhetoric that emphasizes the importance of 'the people' as a unified, virtuous entity, criticizes or depicts elites, establishment, or institutions as corrupt or out of touch, and frames political issues as a moral or existential struggle between the common citizens and the corrupt elite. Populist language often includes appeals to national pride, collective identity, and emotional language that positions the leader or movement as the true voice of the 'people.'
populism_example_1: We've learned the concerns of tens of thousands of Americans in the communities where people live and work. And based on the first days of our journey, I am all the more certain that the American people want this nation to become once again the great and good land it ought to be. The people are tired of war and government by the special interests.
populism_example_2: Incidentally, after such a welcome as this, may I just say, in the light of an article that was written recently, that Pat and I are going to go away from this town saying, "We like St. Joseph." And now, if I may ask you to consider with me for a moment--I know that you're standing and some of you can't even hear, or perhaps see--but if you will consider with me for a few moments some of the things we ought to be thinking about as we select the next president and the next vice president of this country.
populism_example_3: What do they respect? What do they understand? Well, first of all, they understand firmness. We must never make a concession to them without getting a concession in return.
exclusion_criteria: A document is classified as non-populist if it employs formal, policy-oriented, or neutral language that emphasizes institutional, diplomatic, or policy details without framing issues as a moral or existential struggle between 'the people' and elites. It avoids emotional appeals, anti-elite rhetoric, and simplifications that cast politics as a moral battle of the common citizens against a corrupt establishment.
non_populism_example_1: There is some very important business before our nation, as you all know, and it encourages me to think that these many groups we see all the time have a strong feeling we had better leave the management of our affairs in the hands of the Democratic party. And one reason for this is that it has become harder and harder instead of easier and easier to tell precisely what the Republican party stands for in this campaign. We know where they stand on the matter of a new labor relations law, for example. That is precisely where they stood for the past five years. That is an old Republican position.
non_populism_example_2: Mr. Chairman, I just happened to run across one thing that a group was doing in some town in Illinois which is illustrative of what I mean by the variety of possibilities. They were merely beautifying the state highway at the access point of the city, where it began to come into the city. And where it had been shabby and ugly and messy they were cleaning it up around there and developing a picnic area--that sort of thing--and an infinite variety of things. Also, of course, from the point of view of the public official, it is a wonderful access point to communities.
non_populism_example_3: The Achilles heel of any nation is spiritual poverty. Aggressive nations seek out such weakness in the same way a bully seeks out a weakling for his attack. There are national bullies yet in this world, ready to seize upon signs of weakness in our American spirit--our faith, our confidence, our determination.
decision_rules: In cases where a document contains emotional, moral, or moralistic language emphasizing 'the people' as a virtuous, unified entity, criticizes or depicts elites or institutions as corrupt or out of touch, and frames issues as a moral or existential struggle between 'the people' and the establishment, it should be classified as populist. When a document is policy-focused, neutral, or emphasizes institutional or diplomatic details without framing issues as a moral battle or emphasizing the moral virtue of 'the people,' it should be classified as non-populist. Ambiguous cases should be resolved by prioritizing the presence of emotional appeals, anti-elite rhetoric, and the us-versus-them framing characteristic of populism.
